summary:
North Jeolla province has no separate local legislation on gender identity or gender expression. The framework a visitor stands under is the national one of South Korea: being transgender is not criminalised, consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, and the only criminalisation in this field sits in the armed forces, where Military Criminal Act article 92-6 punishes consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available in the province and no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 the Yeongdong regional court approved a change of registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is contrary to law to determine gender change on the basis of surgery and that judicial guidelines prescribing surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life in accordance with their gender identity. Because the ruling applies province-wide as national law, a visitor to North Jeolla can seek court approval to change registered sex through the local courts on the same terms.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to use public restrooms. On 22 July 2024 an appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. That ruling binds North Jeolla as national law.

The practical difficulty trans people report in this area is documented. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41 per cent used a restroom belonging to a gender other than their own, 39 per cent avoided food and drink in order to reduce restroom needs, and 36 per cent simply went without using a restroom. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won in damages against a beauty academy that had prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom.

Against that protection, the wider legal environment carries gaps that matter to a visitor. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in South Korea, so services, employment and accommodation offer no statutory protection on those grounds. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult, and the National Human Rights Commission flagged this blind spot in November 2023. There is no same-sex marriage, which affects a visitor travelling with a partner, although the Constitutional Court issued a landmark 2024 ruling extending recognition of same-sex partners' rights in the specific area of healthcare.

No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources, and no incident involving trans people is documented within North Jeolla itself. Organised conservative opposition to LGBT rights remains active, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society.
tangentialFactors:
The two principal rulings shaping trans visitors' expectations in North Jeolla both arose outside the province. The surgery-free registered-sex ruling came from the Yeongdong regional court, and the restroom ruling was decided in Seoul before being finalised on appeal; neither is a provincial initiative, and both travel with the person rather than remaining local to the court that issued them.

The Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, decision on the beauty academy shows the direction of the courts on restroom exclusion, but it also marks out the setting in which exclusion tends to be litigated: private educational and training premises rather than public facilities. A trans visitor to North Jeolla should expect the judicial standard to hold in principle while recognising that enforcement depends on someone bringing a claim.

The gap between the legal standard and reported practice is measurable. The National Human Rights Commission survey suggests that large minorities of trans people continue to restrict their own food, drink and restroom use rather than rely on legal protection, which indicates that the 300,000 won award, symbolic by design, has not changed day-to-day conduct on its own.

Comparatively, South Korea's record is one of partial progress. It recognises transgender people's legal status without surgery, it has a judicially enforced restroom right, and it maintains free media and civil society space assessed positively by Human Rights Watch. At the same time it lacks a national anti-discrimination statute, has no same-sex marriage, and retains a military criminalisation provision upheld as recently as 2023. Organised conservative opposition remains a live political presence rather than a marginal one.
localsOnly:
Residents of North Jeolla stand under the same national rulings as visitors, and the province has no local ordinance that either strengthens or weakens them. A North Jeolla resident assigned male at birth can apply to the local courts to change registered sex without sex-reassignment surgery, since the Yeongdong ruling removed the surgical prerequisite as national law and left the older surgery-based guidelines as reference rather than criteria.

Police advice to avoid public restrooms is itself actionable. A resident who is told by police to stay out of restrooms matching their gender can rely on the appellate holding that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right, with the state liable in damages, as it was in the finalised 300,000 won award.

Exclusion from premises is a recognised ground of claim. The 7 million won award against the beauty academy in Pohang establishes that a private institution barring a transgender person from its restroom can be ordered to pay damages.

Resident-facing services remain patchier than the courts. There are no statutory protections against discrimination in employment, housing or services on grounds of gender identity, and the Ministry of Health and Welfare has declined to produce hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, a gap the National Human Rights Commission identified in November 2023. Changing registered sex also touches family law: the Supreme Court has permitted a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.
outOfScopeNotes:
These sources contain no data on conditions specific to North Jeolla. No incident involving a trans visitor or resident is documented within the province, and the absence of such records should be read as a lack of reporting rather than as evidence of safety or of harm.

The province-level picture is unresolved on several points. Nothing in the inventory states how frequently local courts in North Jeolla have applied the surgery-free standard, how local police forces train officers on restroom access, or whether any North Jeolla employer, school or hospital has been the subject of a claim on gender-identity grounds.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare within the province is not sourced. The inventory records the national ministry's refusal to draft transgender hospitalisation guidelines and the National Human Rights Commission's identification of the gap, but it does not describe what care is in fact available in North Jeolla, its cost, or any waiting time.

Local political context is also unaddressed. The inventory notes that organised conservative opposition is active nationally and cites Human Rights Watch on documented discrimination, but it does not record any North Jeolla-specific demonstration, council debate or counter-demonstration involving LGBT rights, nor any local equality ordinance or its absence on the books.
